contentBlocks.body: ORDER BY sorts the result. Each sort key can be ASC (the default) or DESC, and later keys only break ties left by earlier ones. Paging then skips some rows and takes the next few. The syntax differs by database, but the meaning is the same.

contentBlocks.code:
-- SQL Server (and the SQL standard)
SELECT id, name, price
FROM products
ORDER BY price DESC, id ASC
OFFSET 20 ROWS FETCH NEXT 10 ROWS ONLY;   -- page 3 of 10 rows

-- PostgreSQL, SQLite, MySQL
SELECT id, name, price
FROM products
ORDER BY price DESC, id ASC
LIMIT 10 OFFSET 20;

-- SQL Server shorthand for the first N rows
SELECT TOP (10) id, name, price FROM products ORDER BY price DESC, id;

contentBlocks.body: Always finish ORDER BY with a unique column (usually the primary key). If ten products share the same price, `ORDER BY price` alone lets the database order those ten differently on each request, so rows can repeat or vanish between pages.

OFFSET paging is simple, but the database still has to walk past every skipped row, so page 5,000 is slow. For deep or infinite-scroll paging use keyset (seek) pagination: remember the last row's sort values and ask for the rows after them, which an index on (price, id) can answer directly.

contentBlocks.code:
-- Keyset pagination: the next page after the last row shown (price 19.99, id 482)
SELECT TOP (10) id, name, price
FROM products
WHERE price < 19.99 OR (price = 19.99 AND id > 482)
ORDER BY price DESC, id ASC;

knowledgeItems.prompt: A product list pages with `ORDER BY price OFFSET @skip ROWS FETCH NEXT 20 ROWS ONLY`. Users report the same product showing up on two pages. What is the best fix?

choices: Add a unique tie-breaker: ORDER BY price, id
payload.answer: Add a unique tie-breaker: ORDER BY price, id
payload.explanation: Rows with equal prices have no defined order, so each page query may order them differently. A unique final sort key makes the order total and the pages stable.

knowledgeItems.prompt: Why is keyset (seek) pagination faster than OFFSET for page 10,000?

choices: It caches previous pages in the database
It seeks straight to the last-seen key in an index instead of reading and discarding every skipped row
payload.answer: It seeks straight to the last-seen key in an index instead of reading and discarding every skipped row
payload.explanation: OFFSET n still produces and throws away n rows. A WHERE on the sort key lets an index on those columns start exactly where the previous page ended.
